items.text: Direct limits: sums, cokernels
Duals: products $\to$ sums; kernels $\to$ cokernels of double arrows; fibre products $\to$ amalgamated sums; final object $\to$ initial object.
$\mathbf{Sets}\not\simeq\mathbf{Sets}^{\circ}$: the two kinds of limit are not symmetric.
In $\mathbf{Sets}$: sums = disjoint unions; initial object = $\varnothing$ (not the point).
Cokernel of $u,v\colon E\rightrightarrows F$: quotient of $F$ by the equivalence relation generated by
\operatorname{im}\bigl((u,v)\colon E\to F\times F\bigr)
\operatorname{coker}(u,v)=F/R,\qquad R=\text{equivalence relation generated by } \{(u(e),v(e))\}
Algebraic categories (groups, abelian groups, modules): all limits exist; direct limits are « free » constructions.
G\ast H\ \ \text{(sum of groups = free product)};\qquad \underbrace{\mathbf Z\ast\cdots\ast\mathbf Z}_{n}=F_n
Inverse limits commute with the forgetful functor to sets; direct limits do not (sums are not disjoint unions).
Same gap of difficulty in sheaves: direct limits exist but are less trivial than inverse limits.
Functors with values in a category $S$
Whenever a type of limit exists in $S$, it exists in $\operatorname{Hom}(C,S)$ and is computed componentwise — inverse or direct.
\operatorname{Hom}(C^{\circ},S)^{\circ}=\operatorname{Hom}(C,S^{\circ})
So direct limits of presheaves exist, computed componentwise from those in $\mathbf{Sets}$.
\Bigl(\coprod_i F_i\Bigr)^{P}(U)=\coprod_i F_i(U)\qquad\text{(sum in presheaves)}
Sheaves are not stable under direct limits
$\operatorname{Top}(X)\subset$ presheaves is stable under no kind of direct limit (empty sum, sum of two, cokernel...).
Yet direct limits exist in $\operatorname{Top}(X)$: they need more work.
Example: the final presheaf $U\mapsto\{*\}$, i.e. the étale space $X\xrightarrow{\mathrm{id}}X$.
(X\sqcup^{P} X)(U)=\{*\}\sqcup\{*\}=\{1,2\}\ \text{ for every } U
Constant presheaf with two elements; transition maps constant. Not a sheaf.
A sheaf has exactly one element on $\varnothing$ (empty covering).
F(\varnothing)=\{*\}\quad\text{for a sheaf } F
Empty sum: $U\mapsto\varnothing$ — again not a sheaf, since $F(\varnothing)$ is empty.
The associated sheaf
Sheaves $F_i$ with arrows $F(\varphi)$. Take $P=\varinjlim^{P} F_i$ in presheaves.
A coherent family $F_i\to G$ ($G$ a sheaf) amounts to one arrow $P\to G$:
\varinjlim_i F_i\ \text{in sheaves represents}\quad G\mapsto \operatorname{Hom}(P,G)
General problem: is $G\mapsto\operatorname{Hom}(P,G)$, $\operatorname{Top}(X)\to\mathbf{Sets}$, representable, for an arbitrary presheaf $P$?
P\longrightarrow\tilde P,\qquad \operatorname{Hom}_{\text{sheaves}}(\tilde P,G)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\operatorname{Hom}_{\text{presheaves}}(P,G)
$\tilde P$ = the sheaf associated to $P$ (a « sheaf envelope »).
Theorem
Every presheaf $P$ has an associated sheaf $\tilde P$, unique up to unique isomorphism.
Proof: Godement; SGA 4, vol. 1, exposé II (for sites). Not given — « one can forget it ».
Consequence: direct limits of sheaves = presheaf limit, then associated sheaf.
Stalks of $P$ and $\tilde P$ agree.
Direct limits of étale spaces
Sum of $F_i$: disjoint union with the sum topology; each $F_i$ open, with its own topology. Étale over $X$ (union of open étale pieces).
It is a sum in all spaces, a fortiori in spaces over $X$ and in étale spaces.
Cokernel of $u,v\colon F\rightrightarrows G$ (étale): take $G/R$ with the quotient topology.
G\to G/R\to X\qquad R=\text{equivalence relation generated by } (u(f),v(f))
$G/R$ is étale (easy exercise), and a cokernel in all spaces, hence in étale spaces.
Sums and cokernels suffice to build every direct limit.
Exactness properties
$\operatorname{Top}(X)$ behaves like $\mathbf{Sets}$ for exactness: arbitrary direct limits, but only finite inverse limits.
Caveat: infinite products of epimorphisms.
In $\mathbf{Sets}$ a product of surjections is surjective; not so for sheaves.
Method: (1) inverse limits of sheaves are argumentwise; (2) direct limits: argumentwise, then $\alpha$.
\alpha\colon \hat{\mathcal O}\to\operatorname{Top}(X),\qquad P\mapsto\tilde P
\operatorname{Hom}(P,i(F))=\operatorname{Hom}(\alpha(P),F)\qquad(\alpha\dashv i)
$\alpha$ is a left adjoint: it commutes with all direct limits.
Theorem (with the construction): $\alpha$ is left exact — commutes with finite products and kernels of pairs.
\alpha(P\times Q)=\alpha P\times\alpha Q,\qquad \alpha\ker(u,v)=\ker(\alpha u,\alpha v)
Admitted (needs stalks). This explains why finite inverse limits carry over from sets, infinite ones not.
Example 1: base change and cokernels
In sheaves over $H$: $F\overset{u}{\underset{v}{\rightrightarrows}}G$, with cokernel $K$, $p\colon G\to K$.
\begin{CD} F @>{u}>> G @>{p}>> K\\ @VVV @VVV @VVV\\ H @= H @= H \end{CD}
Base change along $H'\to H$: $F',G',K'$.
\begin{CD} F' @>{u'}>> G' @>{p'}>> K' \end{CD}
Claim: if the first diagram is exact, so is the second — base change commutes with cokernels (clear in sets).
$K=\tilde{\bar K}$, with $\bar K$ the cokernel in presheaves.
In presheaves, base change commutes with cokernels (argumentwise). So $\bar K'$ = coker in presheaves.
K'=K\times_H H'=\widetilde{\bar K}\times_H H' =\widetilde{\bar K\times_H H'}=\widetilde{\bar K'}
by left exactness of $\alpha$ ($H'$ already a sheaf).
Example 2: base change and sums
Objects $F_i$ over $F$, with sum $S=\coprod F_i$ (over $F$).
F_i'=F_i\times_F F',\qquad S'=S\times_F F'
Question: is $S'=\coprod F'_i$? Then « sums commute with base change ».
True in sets (disjoint unions are fibrewise); only finite inverse limits (fibre products) are used, so true for sheaves.
Example 3: equivalence relations and quotients
Quotient object of $F$: an epimorphism $F\to G$, up to isomorphism of $G$.
Equivalence relation on $F$: a subobject of $F\times F$ (graph of a relation)...
R\subset F\times F\ \ \text{reflexive, symmetric, transitive}
